name: Biomechanical Analysis
title: Biomechanical Analysis
answer: Biomechanical analysis in choreography and motion mapping examines how the human body moves under physical forces, using measurements such as joint angles, ground reaction forces, and muscle activity. It supports choreographers, animators, and movement researchers who want to understand effort, balance, and injury risk in a given sequence. The work often combines motion capture, computer vision, and machine learning to turn recorded movement into structured data. This data can then be mapped to notation systems, animation rigs, or generative models for dance and performance.

sections.body: Biomechanical analysis in choreography and motion mapping examines how the human body moves under physical forces, using measurements such as joint angles, ground reaction forces, and muscle activity. It supports choreographers, animators, and movement researchers who want to understand effort, balance, and injury risk in a given sequence. The work often combines motion capture, computer vision, and machine learning to turn recorded movement into structured data. This data can then be mapped to notation systems, animation rigs, or generative models for dance and performance.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on motion capture systems, which may be optical with reflective markers, inertial with wearable sensors, or markerless using ordinary cameras and pose estimation software. Force plates and electromyography sensors add kinetic and muscle activation data. Computation typically happens on a workstation or cloud instance with a GPU, using biomechanical modeling packages and machine learning frameworks. Data storage and versioning are important because a single session can produce many gigabytes of time series.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The process starts with capturing movement, either in a lab with markers or in the studio with video. Pose estimation models then track body landmarks across frames, and a biomechanical model fits a skeleton with joint centers and segment lengths. From there, inverse dynamics calculates forces and torques at each joint, while machine learning can classify movement quality or predict strain. For choreography, the resulting data is often mapped to Labanotation or used to drive animated characters. Validation against force plates or manual annotation helps confirm accuracy.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area center on performer consent, biometric data privacy, and ownership of motion recordings. Performers should understand how their movement data will be used, stored, and shared, and whether it can be linked back to them. Provenance matters because a model trained on one dancer's motion may not generalize to another body type, leading to biased or unsafe conclusions. Copyright of choreography is a separate layer, and clear agreements about data use help avoid disputes later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real-time feedback, where a dancer or athlete can see biomechanical metrics on a screen as they move. Smartphone cameras and lightweight pose models are making analysis more accessible outside the lab. Generative models may soon propose choreography that respects a performer's physical limits, though that requires careful validation. Standard formats for motion data and clearer ethical guidelines are likely to emerge as the tools spread.
